items.stem: What is the main focus of a reflective commentary?
options: Describing how long you spent writing
Giving your opinion of the topic
Analysing the linguistic and structural choices made in your own writing and their intended effects
Retelling the content of your writing
items.answer: Analysing the linguistic and structural choices made in your own writing and their intended effects
items.markingKey: The commentary analyses choices of form, structure and language, linked to audience and purpose.

items.stem: A student wrote a letter to a newspaper editor arguing against a school phone ban, including the words ‘punishes the responsible majority for the habits of a few’. Explain the intended effect of this choice, as the student might in a reflective commentary.
items.answer: Antithesis: intended to present the ban as unfair.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark, 1 for each of the following up to the maximum: identifies the choice (antithesis); explains the intended effect (present the ban as unfair); links it to the audience (newspaper readers) or purpose.

items.stem: A student wrote a speech to students persuading them to join a school gardening club, including the words ‘No experience required’. Explain the intended effect of this choice, as the student might in a reflective commentary.
items.answer: Reassurance: intended to remove a likely objection and make joining feel easy.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks, 1 for each of the following up to the maximum: identifies the choice (reassurance); explains the intended effect (remove a likely objection and make joining feel easy); links it to the audience (students) or purpose.

items.stem: A student was asked to write a review of a local café for a student website. This is the student’s response: ‘Café Lumo, Kiln Street. Verdict: worth the walk. Tucked behind the bus station, Lumo is tiny – six tables, one overworked espresso machine and a playlist stuck firmly in the 1990s. But the cardamom buns? Life-changing. Soft, sticky and still warm at four o’clock. Service is slow when it’s busy, so don’t come in a hurry. Students get ten per cent off with a card. Three and a half stars.’ Imagine you are this student. Write a paragraph of reflective commentary analysing two of the choices you made, quoting from your writing.
items.answer: I used front-loaded verdict in a minor sentence in ‘Verdict: worth the walk.’ to give busy student readers my judgement immediately, which suits students. I used personification in ‘one overworked espresso machine’ to add humour and make the café feel characterful rather than shabby, which suits students.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks, 1 per valid point: ‘Verdict: worth the walk.’: front-loaded verdict in a minor sentence – intended to give busy student readers my judgement immediately; ‘one overworked espresso machine’: personification – intended to add humour and make the café feel characterful rather than shabby; ‘But the cardamom buns? Life-changing.’: rhetorical question followed by a hyperbolic minor sentence – intended to create a lively, teenage voice and highlight the best item; ‘Soft, sticky and still warm’: tricolon with sibilance – intended to appeal to the senses so readers can almost taste the buns; ‘so don’t come in a hurry’: direct address with an imperative – intended to give practical advice in a friendly tone; ‘Students get ten per cent off with a card.’: content selected for the audience – intended to include the detail that matters most to student readers; analytical terminology; links to audience and purpose.

items.stem: A student was asked to write a script for a 30-second radio advertisement promoting safe e-scooter riding. This is the student’s response: ‘[sound of traffic] VOICE 1 (worried): Is that a scooter on the pavement? VOICE 2 (calm): Not any more. In this city, scooters stay on roads and cycle lanes. Helmet on. One rider. Eighteen plus. VOICE 1: And if you don’t? VOICE 2: Up to three hundred dollars. Ride smart. Ride safe. [ping]’ Imagine you are this student. Write a paragraph of reflective commentary analysing two of the choices you made, quoting from your writing.
items.answer: I used parallel imperatives with alliteration in ‘Ride smart. Ride safe.’ to give a catchy slogan to end the advert, which suits radio listeners. I used sound effect in ‘[sound of traffic]’ to set the scene instantly for listeners who cannot see anything, which suits radio listeners.
items.markingKey: Award up to 3 marks, 1 per valid point: ‘[sound of traffic]’: sound effect – intended to set the scene instantly for listeners who cannot see anything; ‘Is that a scooter on the pavement?’: question-and-answer dialogue – intended to dramatise the problem through two voices; ‘Helmet on. One rider. Eighteen plus.’: compressed minor sentences – intended to make the rules quick and easy to remember by ear; ‘Ride smart. Ride safe.’: parallel imperatives with alliteration – intended to give a catchy slogan to end the advert; analytical terminology; links to audience and purpose.

items.stem: A student was asked to write a blog post by a teenager about living with water restrictions. This is the student’s response: ‘Day nine of the hosepipe ban and my mum has started timing my showers. Four minutes. FOUR. I’m not saying it’s a human-rights issue, but it’s close. Joking aside, it’s weird seeing the park go brown. The fountain in the square has been switched off and the ducks look personally offended. I get it – the reservoirs are at 31 per cent. But maybe fix the leaky pipes first?’ Imagine you are this student. Write a paragraph of reflective commentary analysing three of the choices you made, quoting from your writing.
items.answer: I used personification in ‘the ducks look personally offended’ to make the effects of the drought vivid and funny, which suits teenage readers. I used time marker as an opening in ‘Day nine of the hosepipe ban’ to give a diary-like immediacy and a personal angle, which suits teenage readers. I used ironic hyperbole in ‘I’m not saying it’s a human-rights issue, but it’s close.’ to mock my own overreaction so readers laugh with me, which suits teenage readers.
items.markingKey: Award up to 4 marks, 1 per valid point: ‘Day nine of the hosepipe ban’: time marker as an opening – intended to give a diary-like immediacy and a personal angle; ‘Four minutes. FOUR.’: minor sentences with capitals – intended to mimic exasperated speech and create comedy; ‘I’m not saying it’s a human-rights issue, but it’s close.’: ironic hyperbole – intended to mock my own overreaction so readers laugh with me; ‘the ducks look personally offended’: personification – intended to make the effects of the drought vivid and funny; ‘But maybe fix the leaky pipes first?’: rhetorical question – intended to end with a pointed criticism in a casual tone; analytical terminology; links to audience and purpose.

items.stem: A student was asked to write a letter to a newspaper editor arguing against a school phone ban. This is the student’s response: “Dear Editor, Your editorial ‘Pocket the Phones’ (12 May) makes a confident case, but it overlooks the students it claims to protect. For many young carers, a phone is not a distraction; it is a lifeline. Banning phones outright punishes the responsible majority for the habits of a few. Surely teaching students to manage technology is better than pretending it does not exist? Yours faithfully, Ines Duarte” Write a reflective commentary on this response, analysing the choices of form, structure and language and their intended effects.
items.answer: Indicative content: ‘Dear Editor,’ (formal salutation): to follow the conventions of a letter to a newspaper; “Your editorial ‘Pocket the Phones’ (12 May)” (reference to the original text): to make clear what I am responding to; ‘a phone is not a distraction; it is a lifeline’ (antithesis with metaphor): to reframe the phone as essential for some students; ‘punishes the responsible majority for the habits of a few’ (antithesis): to present the ban as unfair; ‘Surely teaching students to manage technology is better than pretending it does not exist?’ (rhetorical question): to leave readers with a challenge they find hard to reject; form conventions of a letter; audience: newspaper readers.
items.markingKey: Level-marked out of 10 (AO3 analysis of own linguistic choices, with comparison where required). Level 5 (9–10): perceptive, precise analysis of specific choices of form, structure and language, each linked to audience and purpose with apt quotation from own writing; insightful comparison with the stimulus where required; Level 4 (7–8): clear analysis of a range of choices with relevant quotation and effects; comparison developed where required; Level 3 (5–6): some analysis of choices with some quotation; effects stated rather than explored; comparison partial; Level 2 (3–4): identifies a few choices; mostly narrates the writing process; little quotation; Level 1 (1–2): little analysis; general or irrelevant comment. Indicative content: ‘Dear Editor,’ (formal salutation): to follow the conventions of a letter to a newspaper; “Your editorial ‘Pocket the Phones’ (12 May)” (reference to the original text): to make clear what I am responding to; ‘a phone is not a distraction; it is a lifeline’ (antithesis with metaphor): to reframe the phone as essential for some students; ‘punishes the responsible majority for the habits of a few’ (antithesis): to present the ban as unfair; ‘Surely teaching students to manage technology is better than pretending it does not exist?’ (rhetorical question): to leave readers with a challenge they find hard to reject; form conventions of a letter; audience: newspaper readers.

items.stem: A student was asked to write a travel blog entry written at the end of a day’s trekking. This is the student’s response: “Altitude: 3,900 metres. Mood: somewhere between joy and nausea. Today we climbed for seven hours and I genuinely thought my lungs had resigned. Then the clouds split and there it was – the whole valley laid out like a map someone had painted in gold. Our guide just smiled and said, ‘Every day, the same. Every day, new.’ I’m going to think about that for a while.” Write a reflective commentary on this response, analysing the choices of form, structure and language and their intended effects.
items.answer: Indicative content: ‘Altitude: 3,900 metres. Mood: somewhere between joy and nausea.’ (header-style noun phrases): to parody a log entry and set a humorous tone at once; ‘my lungs had resigned’ (personification): to convey exhaustion with humour; ‘like a map someone had painted in gold’ (simile): to capture the beauty of the view; “‘Every day, the same. Every day, new.’” (direct speech with a paradox): to let the guide’s wisdom carry the reflective ending; ‘I’m going to think about that for a while.’ (reflective ending): to leave readers with a thoughtful, unresolved note; form conventions of a blog; audience: followers of a travel blog.
items.markingKey: Level-marked out of 12 (AO3 analysis of own linguistic choices, with comparison where required). Indicative content: ‘Altitude: 3,900 metres. Mood: somewhere between joy and nausea.’ (header-style noun phrases): to parody a log entry and set a humorous tone at once; ‘my lungs had resigned’ (personification): to convey exhaustion with humour; ‘like a map someone had painted in gold’ (simile): to capture the beauty of the view; “‘Every day, the same. Every day, new.’” (direct speech with a paradox): to let the guide’s wisdom carry the reflective ending; ‘I’m going to think about that for a while.’ (reflective ending): to leave readers with a thoughtful, unresolved note; form conventions of a blog; audience: followers of a travel blog.

items.stem: A student wrote a short tribute to a closing local shop for a community newsletter. The response includes: (1) ‘every customer’s name and most of their mistakes’ (2) ‘Thank you, Mr Mendes.’ (3) “‘Ah, you need a washer, not a new tap.’” Writing as the student, analyse each choice and its intended effect on local residents.
items.answer: I used humorous anticlimax in ‘every customer’s name and most of their mistakes’ to add affectionate humour, which suits local residents. I used direct address in a minor sentence in ‘Thank you, Mr Mendes.’ to end with a personal, community-wide thank-you, which suits local residents. I used direct speech in “‘Ah, you need a washer, not a new tap.’” to give Mr Mendes a warm, recognisable voice, which suits local residents.
items.markingKey: Award up to 5 marks: up to 2 marks for each of the following, according to how fully it is developed and supported: (1) humorous anticlimax: to add affectionate humour; (2) direct address in a minor sentence: to end with a personal, community-wide thank-you; (3) direct speech: to give Mr Mendes a warm, recognisable voice; credit any other valid, supported point. 1 mark for each accurately named choice and 1 for each explained effect.

items.stem: In a commentary that compares your writing with the stimulus text, what should you mainly compare?
options: The handwriting of the two texts
Choices of form, structure and language and the reasons for them
Which text is longer
Which text you prefer
items.answer: Choices of form, structure and language and the reasons for them
items.markingKey: Comparison explains how and why your text differs from or resembles the stimulus.

items.stem: A student wrote a travel blog entry written at the end of a day’s trekking, based on Text A, an extract from a travel memoir about trekking to a mountain monastery. The stimulus includes ‘like a cruel joke’; the student wrote ‘like a map someone had painted in gold’. Explain the similarity or difference between these choices and the reason for it.
items.answer: The stimulus simile expresses frustration; mine expresses wonder.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark, 1 for each of the following up to the maximum: identifies the similarity or difference; refers to both quotations; explains it in terms of form, audience or purpose.

items.stem: A student wrote a short fundraising leaflet for a school sponsored walk, based on Text A, a fundraising email from a children’s hospital charity. The stimulus includes ‘Sign up today, and we will send you a free training plan’; the student wrote ‘• Get sponsored by family and friends’. Explain the similarity or difference between these choices and the reason for it.
items.answer: Both end with practical calls to action; mine uses bullet points instead of continuous prose.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks, 1 for each of the following up to the maximum: identifies the similarity or difference; refers to both quotations; explains it in terms of form, audience or purpose.

items.stem: Read Text B, an editorial in a national newspaper, ‘Pocket the Phones’. ‘The evidence is now difficult to ignore. In schools that have removed smartphones from the school day, teachers report calmer corridors, fewer incidents of online bullying and, in several studies, modest gains in test scores. Of course, a ban is not a cure-all; determined pupils will always find a way, and parents understandably want to be able to reach their children. But these are problems of management, not of principle. Children deserve a few hours each day in which their attention belongs to them rather than to an algorithm. Schools should pocket the phones – and keep them pocketed.’ A student was asked to write a letter to a newspaper editor arguing against a school phone ban. This is the student’s response: “Dear Editor, Your editorial ‘Pocket the Phones’ (12 May) makes a confident case, but it overlooks the students it claims to protect. For many young carers, a phone is not a distraction; it is a lifeline. Banning phones outright punishes the responsible majority for the habits of a few. Surely teaching students to manage technology is better than pretending it does not exist? Yours faithfully, Ines Duarte” Compare two of the student’s choices with choices in the stimulus text, explaining the reasons for the similarities and differences.
items.answer: Both use antithesis to reframe the argument. The stimulus ends with a firm modal recommendation; I end with a rhetorical question.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks, 1 per valid point: ‘a phone is not a distraction; it is a lifeline’ v. ‘problems of management, not of principle’: both use antithesis to reframe the argument; ‘Surely teaching students to manage technology’ v. ‘Schools should pocket the phones’: the stimulus ends with a firm modal recommendation; I end with a rhetorical question; ‘makes a confident case, but it overlooks’ v. ‘Of course, a ban is not a cure-all’: both use concession, but I concede the editorial’s confidence before attacking it; comparative connectives used; reasons linked to audience, form or purpose.

items.stem: Read Text A, a review from a city magazine’s food column. ‘Arrive hungry and leave your diet at home. The new night market on Harbour Road is loud, cramped and gloriously chaotic, and I loved almost every minute. The star is a tiny stall run by two sisters who fold dumplings so fast their hands blur; their pork-and-chive parcels (six for a very reasonable price) are worth the twenty-minute queue alone. The grilled corn was a disappointment – charred outside, oddly cold within – and seating is a battle you will probably lose. Still, for sheer energy there is nothing like it in the city. Four stars.’ A student was asked to write a review of a local café for a student website. This is the student’s response: ‘Café Lumo, Kiln Street. Verdict: worth the walk. Tucked behind the bus station, Lumo is tiny – six tables, one overworked espresso machine and a playlist stuck firmly in the 1990s. But the cardamom buns? Life-changing. Soft, sticky and still warm at four o’clock. Service is slow when it’s busy, so don’t come in a hurry. Students get ten per cent off with a card. Three and a half stars.’ Compare two of the student’s choices with choices in the stimulus text, explaining the reasons for the similarities and differences.
items.answer: Both end with a star rating, a convention of reviews. The stimulus opens with playful imperatives, whereas my review opens with a verdict for quick reading.
items.markingKey: Award up to 3 marks, 1 per valid point: ‘Three and a half stars.’ v. ‘Four stars.’: both end with a star rating, a convention of reviews; ‘Verdict: worth the walk.’ v. ‘Arrive hungry and leave your diet at home.’: the stimulus opens with playful imperatives, whereas my review opens with a verdict for quick reading; ‘Life-changing.’ v. ‘fold dumplings so fast their hands blur’: both use hyperbole to praise the food; comparative connectives used; reasons linked to audience, form or purpose.

items.stem: Nadia wrote a speech to students persuading them to join a school gardening club, adapting Text A, a speech by a city councillor at a residents’ meeting launching a rooftop-garden scheme. Compare the pairs of choices below and evaluate how successfully the student has adapted the stimulus for students: (1) stimulus ‘Look up when you leave tonight.’ – student ‘Hands up if you have ever eaten a tomato you grew yourself.’ (2) stimulus ‘grew four hundred kilos of vegetables’ – student ‘We need twenty volunteers’ (3) stimulus ‘turn this grey city green’ – student ‘Let’s grow something.’
items.answer: (1) Both open with an imperative that asks listeners to do something physical. (2) The stimulus uses figures as evidence of success; I use a figure as a target. (3) Both end with a short slogan, but mine is plainer and more conversational for a student audience. Evaluation: the adaptations suit the new form and audience.
items.markingKey: Award up to 4 marks, 1 per valid point: (1) both open with an imperative that asks listeners to do something physical; (2) the stimulus uses figures as evidence of success; I use a figure as a target; (3) both end with a short slogan, but mine is plainer and more conversational for a student audience; an evaluative judgement on the success of the adaptation; reference to audience and form.

In the order in which you wrote the piece, sentence by sentence

items.stem: A student was asked to write a short tribute to a closing local shop for a community newsletter. This is the student’s response: “After forty-one years, Mendes Hardware will sell its last box of nails on Saturday. For generations of DIY disasters, Mr Mendes was the calm voice at the counter: ‘Ah, you need a washer, not a new tap.’ He knew every customer’s name and most of their mistakes. The shelves are emptying now, but the advice he gave away free will last longer than any of it. Thank you, Mr Mendes.” You are planning the student’s reflective commentary. Write a concluding sentence linking your choices to your purpose.

items.stem: In a commentary on a script for a 30-second radio advertisement promoting safe e-scooter riding, a student writes: ‘I chose words that were good for the text.’ Explain why this is weak, and rewrite it using evidence from the student’s text: ‘[sound of traffic] VOICE 1 (worried): Is that a scooter on the pavement? VOICE 2 (calm): Not any more. In this city, scooters stay on roads and cycle lanes. Helmet on. One rider. Eighteen plus. VOICE 1: And if you don’t? VOICE 2: Up to three hundred dollars. Ride smart. Ride safe. [ping]’
items.answer: Weakness: it gives no quotation from the student’s own writing. Improved: I used sound effect in ‘[sound of traffic]’ to set the scene instantly for listeners who cannot see anything, which suits radio listeners.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark, 1 for each of the following up to the maximum: identifies the weakness (no quotation from own writing); a rewrite that quotes a specific choice; the rewrite explains an effect on the audience.

items.stem: In a commentary on a script for a 30-second radio advertisement promoting safe e-scooter riding, a student writes: ‘First I planned it, then I wrote it, then I checked it.’ Explain why this is weak, and rewrite it using evidence from the student’s text: ‘[sound of traffic] VOICE 1 (worried): Is that a scooter on the pavement? VOICE 2 (calm): Not any more. In this city, scooters stay on roads and cycle lanes. Helmet on. One rider. Eighteen plus. VOICE 1: And if you don’t? VOICE 2: Up to three hundred dollars. Ride smart. Ride safe. [ping]’
items.answer: Weakness: it narrates the writing process instead of analysing choices. Improved: I used question-and-answer dialogue in ‘Is that a scooter on the pavement?’ to dramatise the problem through two voices, which suits radio listeners.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks, 1 for each of the following up to the maximum: identifies the weakness (narrates the writing process); a rewrite that quotes a specific choice; the rewrite explains an effect on the audience.

items.stem: A student was asked to write a blog post by a teenager about living with water restrictions. This is the student’s response: ‘Day nine of the hosepipe ban and my mum has started timing my showers. Four minutes. FOUR. I’m not saying it’s a human-rights issue, but it’s close. Joking aside, it’s weird seeing the park go brown. The fountain in the square has been switched off and the ducks look personally offended. I get it – the reservoirs are at 31 per cent. But maybe fix the leaky pipes first?’ You are planning the student’s reflective commentary. Write a concluding sentence linking your choices to your purpose.
items.answer: A conclusion that links the choices to the purpose of the text.
items.markingKey: 1 mark link; 1 mark clarity [2]

items.stem: A student was asked to write a short tribute to a closing local shop for a community newsletter. This is the student’s response: “After forty-one years, Mendes Hardware will sell its last box of nails on Saturday. For generations of DIY disasters, Mr Mendes was the calm voice at the counter: ‘Ah, you need a washer, not a new tap.’ He knew every customer’s name and most of their mistakes. The shelves are emptying now, but the advice he gave away free will last longer than any of it. Thank you, Mr Mendes.” Write a well-structured reflective commentary on this response. Organise it by choices or frameworks, support each point with quotation and explain each effect.
items.answer: Indicative content: overview of audience, purpose and form; paragraphs organised by framework or choice; ‘After forty-one years’ (time-span opening): to establish the shop’s place in local history; ‘its last box of nails’ (concrete detail): to make the closure feel real and specific; “‘Ah, you need a washer, not a new tap.’” (direct speech): to give Mr Mendes a warm, recognisable voice; ‘every customer’s name and most of their mistakes’ (humorous anticlimax): to add affectionate humour; ‘Thank you, Mr Mendes.’ (direct address in a minor sentence): to end with a personal, community-wide thank-you; comparison with the stimulus where relevant; conclusion.
items.markingKey: Level-marked out of 10 (AO3 analysis of own linguistic choices, with comparison where required). Level 5 (9–10): perceptive, precise analysis of specific choices of form, structure and language, each linked to audience and purpose with apt quotation from own writing; insightful comparison with the stimulus where required; Level 4 (7–8): clear analysis of a range of choices with relevant quotation and effects; comparison developed where required; Level 3 (5–6): some analysis of choices with some quotation; effects stated rather than explored; comparison partial; Level 2 (3–4): identifies a few choices; mostly narrates the writing process; little quotation; Level 1 (1–2): little analysis; general or irrelevant comment.
